newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan seen taking risk loss on forex deposits.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan seen taking risk loss on forex deposits.

text.p: Pakistan's central bank suffered an estimated loss of 38 billion rupees ($945 million) in risk cover on foreign exchange deposits in July-October due to rupee depreciation, analysts and bankers said on Wednesday.
The State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) itself reported a loss of 11.21 billion rupees in 1995/96 (July-June) on the exchange risk cover it provides banks on their forex deposits.

Deputy SBP governor Mehfooz Alam told Reuters the central bank would again incur losses this year, but gave no figures. "Whenever the depreciation is over and above the fee and foreign exchange transaction income, we will incur a loss," he said.
Alam would not say if the SBP planned to raise its fee in proportion to the depreciation to staunch the losses.
Bankers said the SBP would be reluctant to take such a step in case it sparked an outflow of badly needed forex deposits.

"In the first four months of this year the rupee has depreciated by nearly 15 percent, which means the SBP has already lost an estimated 38 billion rupees," research head of Taurus Securities Abid Naqvi said in a report.
He said the losses had been calculated assuming that banks had a total forex deposit base of $8.0 billion.
It was not immediately clear whether any budget provision had been made for the SBP's 1995/96 risk cover losses.
The SBP launched its exchange risk cover scheme in 1990, when exchange controls and restrictions on forex deposits were eased. It was aimed at shoring up depleting forex reserves.

Under the scheme banks raise non-resident and resident forex deposits, swap them with the SBP for an equivalent rupee amount at the spot selling rate and enter a forward purchase contract with the SBP at the same spot rate, bankers said.
Banks pay a forward cover, or hedging, fee to the SBP. This was zero when the scheme began, but now stands at 4.75 percent a year on dollar deposits.
Naqvi said banks have been arbitraging lucratively between low Eurodollar rates and high-yielding rupee-denominated government securities.

The SBP has devalued the rupee 14.29 percent against the dollar since July, slashing 7.86 percent off its dollar value on October 22 as part of an IMF-inspired stabilisation package intended to narrow the budget gap by 40 billion rupees with spending cuts, new taxes and a 10 percent fuel price rise.

Naqvi said the rupee's annual depreciation had fluctuated sharply over the past five years from a high of 16.2 percent in 1993/94 to a low of 2.3 percent in 1994/95 -- when the SBP would have profited as the depreciation was lower than the cover fee.
"On average, however, the depreciation rate over the past five years was close to 8.3 percent per annum, so the SBP has overall lost money on the scheme," he said.
He said the losses sustained were adjusted against the SBP's account for the year and correspondingly reduced its operating surplus contribution to government revenue.
The SBP annual report, released last week, showed the surplus paid by the SBP to the federal government at 13.02 billion rupees in 1995/96 against 18.48 billion in 1994/95.
A foreign banker, who asked not to be named, said the SBP had taken no decision on raising the fee so far, but doing so could help keep losses at manageable levels.
However, foreign banks would then seek compensatory higher returns on government securities, which would raise the cost of government borrowing, he said.
